content.text: {"start": 236.0, "end": 275.0, "segments": [{"start": 236.48, "end": 241.68, "time": "03:56", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "There's also a big loophole in capital gains taxes that the rich exploit called the stepped-up basis."}, {"start": 242.46, "end": 251.42, "time": "04:02", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "If, hypothetically, Warren Buffett were to sell his stock, he'd have to pay capital gains taxes based on his profit, so the cost of the stock minus the original investment."}, {"start": 252.1, "end": 262.64, "time": "04:12", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "But if he holds off selling his entire life, when he dies, whoever inherits the stock and then sells it would only have to pay taxes on what they earned after they inherited it,"}, {"start": 263.52, "end": 266.24, "time": "04:24", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "leaving all those original gains untaxed."}, {"start": 267.2, "end": 273.2, "time": "04:27", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "It's part of what's called buy, borrow, die, and it's one way the richest families avoid paying taxes."}, {"start": 274.02, "end": 283.92, "time": "04:34", "speaker": "speaker_0", "text": "It's this system and the fact that most taxable capital gains are going to the top 1% that lawmakers see changing the capital gains tax as an easy way to tax the rich."}]}

content.text:
John would pay $4.50 per share in capital gains tax.

The video explains the "stepped-up basis" at [03:56–04:24]. Someone who inherits stock and later sells it "would only have to pay taxes on what they earned after they inherited it." Any gains from before the inheritance are never taxed.

- John's basis steps up to the $150 value at Emily's death in 2020. Her original $50 purchase price no longer counts.
- His taxable gain is $180 − $150 = $30 per share.
- At 15%, the tax is $30 × 0.15 = $4.50 per share.

The $100 per share Emily gained between 2005 and 2020 is never taxed. The video calls this a loophole used in "buy, borrow, die" [04:27].

Answer: A
